speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, April 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Richardson for an address to Her Excellency the Governor General in reply to ther speech at the opening of the session.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the speech at the opening of the thirty-fourth Parliament, the Government stated that culture, together with the economy, social affairs and the environment, is one of the essential building blocks of our national identity. At a time when there is a tendency among the nations of the world to regroup in large economic units, when borders established in the 18th and 19th century are being erased to allow for the necessary circulation of goods, services and information, creators and artists, whom we may have taken for granted in the past, are now becoming increasinly important to their respective communities.
We are entering the so-called information society, which throughout the world is bringing about a likeness in our goods and services. Creators, however, are doing the exact opposite. They explore, search and experiment and in doing so, express what makes them and what makes us unique. Our identity is reflected in their works.
How to reconcile this development of our authentic cultural uniqueness with the imperatives of the information society is the most important challenge we have to meet as Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, Canada's cultural reality is made up of four components. First, a necessary technological infrastructure: our telecommunications; second, a broadcasting system that must reflect what we are; third, an
aggregate of cultural industries: publishing, films, recording and design which, unfortunately, do not enjoy a normal, healthy existence as far as their operations are concerned; and finally, the artists and creators without whom none of this is possible and who form the ever fragile foundation of this system.
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Communications assumes the Government's responsibility for these four components. I will touch on them briefly.
First, the telecommunications sector. In 1987, this sector contributed nearly $16 billion to our Gross Domestic Product. Telecommunications is one of our economy's fastest growing industries, with an annual growth rate of 8.4 per cent in 1987 and 6.8 per cent last year, compared with 2.3 and 4.8 per cent for Canada's manufacturing industry as a whole.
The telecommunications industry, with 86.5 per cent Canadian ownership and 79 per cent owned by the private sector, is becoming an increasingly important instrument for our economic development. To own and operate an integrated telecommunications system that is universally accessible and to do so at affordable rates has become one of the essential prerequisites for any advanced economy on this planet, and its importance is increasing. It is not surprising that the Japanese have made telecommunications their development priority. Nor is it surprising that the European community has identified telecommunications as a priority prototype sector for integration in the "single market" in 1992. However, the benefits of our telecommunications system and the information it carries are not purely functional. The sector will, and in fact already does, have an impact on the daily lives of all Canadians. It will affect our social and cultural activities and help very substantially to reduce regional disparity.
Twenty years from now, countries that have not taken advantage of technologies such as high definition television, for instance, will no longer be in the running.
In addition to being the main motor of our economy, these technologies, these electronic media which are already partly responsible for disseminating our culture, will also be the main source of job creation in Canada during the next twenty years.

The Address-Mr. Masse
In Canada and all over the world, technologies are already considered an essential tool for ensuring the competitiveness of companies in every field. Not only will they have an enormous impact on the economy, but they will also considerably alter our social reality, education and training programs, and of course the distribution of our cultural products both at home and abroad. The importance of this technological revolution cannot be overstated.
Now, can you tell which country is among the three or four world leaders in the field of technology development? Yes, it's Canada. We are the best there is in a field generally considered to be a key sector, which should ensure our economic development. All we have to do now is to remain the best. Our strength lies in telecommunications which must become a fundamental part of our industrial development in the present state of the economy, where competitiveness is more and more important.
In this race, we start with a definite lead over all the industrialized nations. We must then improve and strengthen our communications infrastructure so as to meet the economic and technological needs of the 21st century. This infrastructure must be used to link Canadians to each other and to the rest of the world.
Broadcasting is the most popular and powerful vehicle for culture available to us now. Statistics Canada has recently published data showing that 99 per cent of all Canadian families own a radio set, 98 per cent have a television set, and more than 50 per cent have a VCR. That should tell us the tremendous power those media have when it comes to the spread of information, the sale of products and services, the influence on public opinion, the making of stars, and especially a chance to give the majority of people the opportunity to share a common experience.
The Government must therefore undertake to ensure that a full selection of quality Canadian programs reflecting our reality and intended directly for us is available in this country. Our political and cultural sovereignty requires it, if we do not want our culture to become marginal in Canada itself.
It is therefore important for our television broadcasting system to give priority to our own television production and for the Government to encourage its growth.
For if television does not show Canadians an image of themselves, if this image is lacking in quality, we can ask how they will strengthen their feeling of belonging. A television set is not just a receiver. It is the primary tool to cement culture in the modern era. As anthropologist Edward T. Hall notes:
The phenomenon of identification is perhaps the most important
psychological aspect of culture, a bridge that links personality to
culture.
In 1985, the cultural sector was the ninth largest manufacturing industry in Canada and earned more than $12 billion.
The cultural sector is the fourth largest employer in Canada. Cultural industries, including broadcasting, provide Canadians with more than 105,000 direct jobs. Some 4,000 people work full time in museums and heritage institutions and about 5,000 work there part time. The sound recording industry provides 15,000 direct jobs, mostly for young people. The labour force is growing faster in the cultural area than in other sectors of the Canadian economy.
In addition, the number of cultural institutions is increasing all the time. From 1972 to 1986, the number of arts organizations subsidized by the Canadian Government increased considerably: from 49 to 197 theatre companies, from 63 to 160 music ensembles, from 11 to 41 dance companies. This remarkable growth shows Canada's cultural vitality!
These figures, impressive as they are, must not hide the problems facing cultural industries that we must solve in the coming years. Those industries, needless to add, are in a state of under-capitalization and more often than not have no access to economies that would enable them to compete here in Canada even with the major producers of mass culture events.
The basic problem of our culture industries is that they are working in a distorted market where they are structurally unable to compete profitably with global-scale firms already in the field.
The Government must step in to allow Canadians to do business in our own land, just as the others do in their own country. Let me mention here the Musicaction Program established by the Department of Communications three years ago, which did much to put the French and English-speaking segments of the record industry on their feet again.

For its part, the film industry must cope with a number of difficulties. Of course, Governments afford our film and TV production a kind of support that is unequalled in any other country, to the tune of nearly $200 million through the activities of large agencies such as Telefilm Canada, the NFB and the CBC, on the one hand and incentives like the capital cost write-off on the other. But we must do more and come up with a series of steps to solve the problems behind the imbalance in the Canadian distribution market, that is to ensure to Canadian distributors the availability of their own market. Right now, our distributors collect only 10 per cent of the total receipts from movie theatres and home videos, even though in 1984 they distributed 28 of the 29 feature films produced in Canada.
As a last example, nearly 80 per cent of book publishers in Canada are Canadians, and they put out nearly 70 per cent of available publications. However, they can fill no more than 35 per cent of the schoolbook, reference book and general material market. Further, most Canadian publishing houses hardly reach the break even point, and in the best of cases only exceed it by 5 or 10 per cent.
It is important therefore to ensure that Canadian products are offered as efficiently as foreign products are on the market. The strength of this country's identity is at stake. The Government of Canada is conscious of the importance of that matter.
But cultural products must be made before they become available on the market. They constitute the output of creative men and women who play a leading or even decisive role in defining and promoting the Canadian identity. Given today's major communication and information networks, these men and women cannot be left to fend for themselves even though they work alone within their own society. To the extent that this society needs them it must ensure their survival. But do they really manage to live off their art? Let us briefly examine the financial predicament of Canada's professional artists.
Every week our creators devote 35 to 40 hours to their art and have to work at something else 10 to 15 hours to make ends meet. Their artistic endeavours barely enable them to survive in a world where, oftentimes, material wealth is the hallmark of success. Canadian annual income statistics indicate that authors earn $15,200, dancers and choreographers $16,800, visual artists $21,500, actors $24,500, and musicians $25,100. No wonder more than half of Canadian creators, when queried,
The Address-Mr. Masse
look upon their artistic activities more as a calling than as a business or a profession!
That being the case, we have to see to it that public authorities give some kind of priority to defending the interests of artists and creators. We see our own reflection when we look at our artists.
With that in mind, Mr. Speaker, we intend-as the Speech from the Throne puts it-to improve the distribution of Canada's cultural products in broadcasting, film and video, and provide our authors with a system which acknowledges the significance of their contribution to the life of our community.
Broadcasting is the most popular and powerful instrument of our identify. The Government is committed to ensuring a complete range of quality Canadian programs that reflect our reality and are aimed at us. In that respect, we will continue implementing our agenda, which calls for a systematic, determined strengthening of the legislative framework of Canadian culture.
It is that spirit that the Broadcasting Bill will be reintroduced in this House, as well as major legislative initiatives in the areas of filmmaking, museums and archeology.
We also intend to propose the implementation of Phase 2 of the Copyright Act, which we feel essential in every way, an innovative approach to Canadian artists' and creators' living conditions.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian culture is the first expression of our identity. It is also and perhaps foremost above all the contribution of Canadians to humanity's artistic values and heritage.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Minister's speech with a great deal of interest. He spoke about telecommunications and transmission policy concerning television as well as radio. He then moved on to talk about the educational end of things as well as the arts community in general.
Since we have Crown corporations such as the CBC, the National Arts Centre and the National Research Council, will the Minister agree that rather than cutting funds from these institutions we should be encouraging them and not taking away from them? I was somewhat shocked to learn through the media that the National Arts Centre Orchestra will be privatized. I also heard some discussion about the possibility of passing on the National Arts Centre to the NCC.

The Address-Mr. Masse
I do not know whether the Minister has had time in the past, present, or will have in the future, to sit down to look at this aspect of Canadian culture in terms of what it really means to Canadians. Look at the idea of the arts and how we can use the arts to promote tourism and encourage economic development. When talking about radio and television transmission, consider how they are connected to research and development.
When the Government sits down to have a sober look at what it is doing in the area of culture, will the Minister be working with his colleagues and pushing them to press ahead in areas such as research and development and culture, that is, ensuring that the content of television and radio transmission will focus more on Canadian culture and content?
I think the Government can really take a leadership role when it comes to the arts community. We are in the best position to take that role by maintaining agencies such as the National Arts Centre and by investing more in terms of incentives. If there are difficulties with some of these agencies, I think the best approach is to sit down with management to try to work out the differences rather than to say that we have had enough and it is time now to pass them on to the private sector. If we do pass these agencies on to the private sector and rely solely on the private sector, eventually what we will end up doing, as a Government, is absolutely nothing. We have a leadership role to play. It is important for the private sector to enter into partnership with the federal Government. However, it is also important that the federal Government stay in place as a watch-dog and be there in terms of playing the role of facilitator with these different agencies in order that Canadian culture and unity be promoted. That is what Canada is all about. Will the Minister comment, please?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. Many matters were raised that could be debated for days.
Let me say first There is no direct link between the amount of money spent in anyone sector and that sector's success or failure. I referred to the Canadian
film sector. Of all Western countries Canada probably has invested directly in film making the most public money-nearly $200 million. And this probably is the sector where Canadians have the most difficulty seeing Canadian productions. Two hundred million dollars for 26 million Canadians. But in our movie theatres, 97 per cent of films seen by Canadians are foreign. Three per cent only are Canadian films. Despite the fact that three agencies-Telefilm Canada, the NFB and to a degree the CBC-are involved in film production. But at the movie theatre level Canadians derive no benefits from that at all. It is not for lack of public money. Would the problem be solved if we were to throw in another $100 million? Absolutely not! The problem is not a monetary one. It's not a funding problem public funds but rather a set up problem, a structural problem in the set up of our Canadian film industry.
This is the reason why we should be cautions, Mr. Speaker, before we ask the Government to invest more money. Throwing more money into a bad policy will not get the positive result we expect. This is why I believe we must work at two levels. Of course a minimum of public effort is needed. In the next few months I will have an opportunity to show that Canadians are making a tremendous effort by investing in their own identity through their culture. Mr. Speaker, I rise today to respond to the Speech from the Throne as a Member of Parliament from an area that lies between London and Sarnia, Ontario. It is a riding that has four Indian reservations within it. I was very disappointed when I read the Speech from the Throne under the theme "A Caring Nation".
I was disappointed because I did not see one word about our native peoples, those native peoples who are today demonstrating in front of this institution on Parliament Hill. They are demonstrating on behalf of their children who are being deprived of an education at the highest level. Certainly at this time in Canadian history such an education is essential to the future not only of our native peoples but of our nation as a whole. This right cannot be limited by Government. This right cannot be held hostage by the federal deficit, a deficit that is being fought on the backs of the poor, the sick, the disadvantaged and the unemployed. If there is any group which needs help under our Unemployment Insurance Program it is our native people who rely on fishing, tourism and other aspects of life that have been built around the social systems which we have in place in Canada.
We have out in front here today Verna Brown of Oneida, Karen Deleary of Muncey, Candess Bressette of Kettle Point with Laura George, Brian Monague, Tammy George, Ron George and Maynard George. We have in our gallery today Wayne Hill, his wife and their two sons. They are here to protest what is happening to the education of native people. They are here to try to convince this Government that their sons deserve an education, an education that should be available to all Canadians, not just the privileged few of families of the elite.
A couple of days ago the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Valcourt) spoke in this House. He said that he will assist business to adapt to changes in our systems brought about by the Free Trade Agreement. In the last few years we have heard a lot concerning bringing about harmonization of regulations between Canada and the United States. When I look at some of the changes that have taken place in the last couple of years, I am shocked that instead of raising the standard on United States products coming into Canada, we are undermining Canadian standards by allowing sub-stan dard products to come in from the United States. In fact
The Address-Mr. Ferguson
the President of Weston Foods said: "Unlike Canadian products shipped south of the border, items coming into Canada from the United States are not stopped at the border if they do not meet federal guidelines".
The Grocery Products Manufacturers estimate there are nearly 300 improperly labelled products on grocery store shelves in Canada at the present time. This is shocking. We have established Canadian standards of great quality that have served this nation well. They are recognized around the world.
I want to give another example of what is happening. In our Canadian beef industry we have various grades of beef that ensure consumers that when they buy Canada Grade A, it is a youthful carcass with tender meat, a shiny bone texture and a minimum fat cover of not less than four millimetres and not more than 19 millimetres. A certain amount of fat is necessary to ensure good quality beef.
I am shocked to learn that there are about one million pounds a week of ungraded-it is called unrolled beefcoming into Canada, beef that is essentially cow beef. I am not suggesting that there is anything wrong with cow beef provided you do not mind the toughness and you do not object to chewing on it for a while. This beef is being offered in our stores without any identification, with nothing to tell the consumers that it is inferior quality. It is being blended with the Canadian beef. That is that we as beef producers from Canada have to compete against. From what I understand only one consumer in 10 will complain. Consequently, consumers are being taken to the cleaners. If you have one consumer who complains, you can rest assured there are 10 unhappy consumers who do not tell their friends and associates where they made their purchase.
We have gone into an agreement with the Americans assuring that any imported goods are stamped with a grade that is equivalent to that of what we have here in Canada, not only to protect the interests of the consumers, but to protect the interests of the purchasers here in Canada. After all the talk we have heard about level playing fields, surely the Government has a responsibility to make sure that these products are labelled with a grade equivalent similar to what we have here in Canada.
To sell this beef under the impression that it is something else can only harm the industry and lead to a drop in consumption. I suggest that this is the most important issue facing the beef industry today in Canada. Measures must be brought in to protect the consumer and the industry as a whole.

The Address-Mr. Ferguson
I am further shocked at the emergence of imported products showing up on store shelves that do not conform to our Canadian quality standards. Surely if this Government is going to continue with harmonious relations with the United States, it should insist that U.S. standards be brought up to ours and not ours be brought down to theirs.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

The next issue I want to speak about very briefly this morning is the removal of oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board without consultation with the Canadian Wheat Board or with the producers. In fact, the Minister has broken the Government's own rules for regulatory reform. I fully realize that this code is not enforceable by law, but the citizen's code of regulatory fairness was established in March, 1986, to give the public access to decision-making before the Government makes regulation changes.
I am sure that the Minister will try to convince us that this commodity of oats only accounts for less than 1 per cent of the value of the Canadian Wheat Board sales. He will try to convince us that it is a very minor issue. But the fact is that if oats go out this year, will wheat and barley follow next year and the year after?
I together with the farmers believe that this is true or else the Minister's resignation would not have been called for. I believe it is the Free Trade Agreement that calls for the free trade movement of grains across our borders when levels of subsidies become equal, and that barley and oats will be next to go. Let me tell you that the subsidy level for oats will be at par this year with that of the United States. For wheat and barley, it will be level next year. It is not much wonder that the farmers of western Canada and eastern Canada are upset that barley has been removed from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. Their information also points out that barley and wheat will have equal subsidies in both countries within a year to a year and a half. When this happens, the farmers of Canada will lose the most sophisticated marketing system in the world, and will be thrown to the mercy of a few multinational companies and the commodity exchanges that have been rocked by recent scandals and investigations.
Just let me quote from a series of questions asked the Ministers of the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board. The first question: What will be the role of the Canadian Wheat Board in the marketing and pricing of wheat with the understanding that import and export authority will no longer be within the Wheat Board mandate? They did not get an answer. Second: What Department or under what Minister will the decisions be made regarding the establishment of the North American price for wheat and equalization of subsidies?
The third question: How much authority will the Canadian Grain Commission have in policing the end use certificate policy? End use certificates will not require the grade of wheat to be indicated. This allows the import of low-grade wheat at lower prices than Canadian wheat of top grade or even lower grade because of quality control disparity trading, creating unfair competition. How will this serious problem be resolved? Certificates will not require the grade of wheat.
I spoke just a moment ago of ungraded beef coming into Canada, what it is doing to our markets and what is happening to consumers who purchase this beef. Now we are facing the same situation with wheat. How much authority will be implemented regarding the import of wheat-based products into Canada, or will there be any authority at all implemented? Who in the federal Government will decide what is a subsidy on either side of the border? Will the federal Government establish a direct payment compensation program to address this discriminatory pricing of wheat other than through stabilization? Will the federal Government permit direct producer input in overseeing price determination domestically, or will it in turn take the route it took with the removal of oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board? In fact, the Government broke its own rules of the citizens code of regulatory fairness.
Those are the questions that are asked by the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board. They had another question that is essential to the continuation of that board. Will the Canadian Wheat Board continue with an initial payment pooling system? If so, how will the initial payment be established? Will the Minister put that in writing?
The wheat producers are asking the Minister to put it in writing because they are not satisfied with the answers so far, if indeed they received any answers at all.


Canadian farmers have a right to know. The Govern ment must respond, if indeed this is a democratic country and if the Minister is interested in the welfare of the producers. Instead, is he only interested in the welfare of a few very large multinational corporations?
All the signs that come from the Government and other sources indicate that the Government is moving to dismantle one of the most sophisticated marketing systems in the world. As further processed products are brought into Canada, many of which are of lower quality and consequently lower priced, Canadian production will have to be cut and food processors will be forced out of business. As the food processors are forced out of business, so will the farmers. Scores are being forced out at this time.
It only takes a few percentage points of surplus to wreck a market and destroy an industry. As the old adage goes, two buyers after one cow means a good market, but one buyer after two cows is a disaster.
I was shocked to see some of the explanations and options being considered by the United States. In fact, in a recent document to the United States Senate Committee on Agriculture and Nutrition, the U.S. Trade Representative laid out the options for negotiating the elimination of the Canadian Wheat Board and wheat product licensing requirements, and explained their preference. This document lays out those preferences. It states:
There are several ways in which the question of restrictive Canadian import licensing of wheat and wheat products may be addressed. The first of these has been incorporated into the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. The FTA provides that when the level of Government support for wheat in the United States becomes equal to or less than the level of Government support in Canada, Canada shall eliminate any import permit requirements for wheat and wheat products originating in the territory of the United States.
That is what is happening to the Canadian wheat producers. When it happens, the Canadian Wheat Board will be stripped of its powers.
In the last two years, I have had scores of farmers ask me what the Government is doing to our marketing system. The dairy farmers of Lambton and Middlesex Counties and the whole poultry industry are realizing that this cruel big business Government is quite prepared to give away their marketing structures for the sake of making a deal at any cost.
The Address-Mr. Ferguson
There are only three lines concerning agriculture in the Speech from the Throne. It referred to the industry as being a drain on the nation's economy. I am a farmer. At this time of year I always look forward with anticipation and optimism to the spring planting season and the year ahead. I look forward to the creation of new plant life and hopefully a bountiful harvest. I resent being told that I am a drain on the nation's treasury.
The Government has thrown us to the vultures in this whole free market economy. There seems to be a double standard in the Government. It is okay for the huge corporations to exert more power on the market-place, but if Canada's farmers try to maintain a countervailing force in the market-place they are told to become more efficient.
When I return home to my riding every week-end, I am shocked at the number of farmers who are coming to me for financial assistance. In fact, in my colleague's riding of Essex-Kent, there are 200 farmers being forced off the farms through Farm Credit Corporation actions alone.
I am proud to be a farmer. I am proud of the role we play in society. But I cannot understand why any Government would possibly contemplate destroying our systems and our quality standards to become part of the law of the jungle.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make some comments on the Throne Speech and the Member's speech. I am pleased that in the Speech from the Throne the Government talked about a strong commitment to a strong economy and recognized the importance of deficit reduction. However, we should not forget that in 1984 our total debt was approximately $200 billion. Now, in 1989, it is $320 billion. Annual interest rates on that debt now consume 31 cents of every dollar of Government revenue, and these payments are putting pressure on the Government's ability to meet other priorities.
Canada has been borrowing money solely to pay the interest from previous borrowings. In order to reverse this trend, expenditures must be reduced and revenue must cover the cost of Government programs.
In the Speech from the Throne the Government talks about tax reform and proposes a new federal sales tax to replace the manufacturers sales tax. This new federal sales tax could be a value added tax, or a tax on consumer goods and services.

This concerns the value added tax and how it affects farmers. I would like to continue.
I would oppose the value added tax for two reasons. First, it would leave less money in the pockets of taxpayers than the present taxation system. Second, it would require additional staff positions to be implemented.
Canadian taxpayers are already over-burdened. In 1984, a study of the value added tax by the United States Department of Treasury estimated that implementation of a value added tax in the United States would require 21,000 staff positions and would cost some $700 million to the United States Treasury. Mr. Speaker, certainly I am against any value added tax as far as farmers are concerned. We have a very difficult time now adjusting our cash flows. That is another added expense to the farm community.
Perhaps I should point out to the hon. gentlemen, that in 1984, when the Government took office, the national debt was $130 billion. It is now at $320 billion, almost double.
We had just gone through a period of recession and had positive growth since December, 1982. Consequently, that deficit and the national debt should have been brought down, not allowed to escalate. I can point out to him that Government expenditures increased dramatically since that time as well.
Two days ago I tabled two petitions in the House. One was on behalf of the dairy farmers in Lambton-Middlesex in southwestern Ontario to point out to the Government that their systems are in jeopardy and the whole industry is in jeopardy. I tabled a petition for beef producers who are upset about the "no-roll", ungraded United States beef coming into this country. If the agriculture industry in Canada is to survive under this Free Trade Agreement, we must go back to the systems we had in place and that have served this industry for many years. We must ensure that the United States raises their standards to our standards and not tear ours down.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to address this House on the Throne Speech. The Throne Speech is a positive plan, a direction for the Thirty-Fourth Parliament. It sets out a plan of objectives and purposes of this Government for the future. This future presents our constituency with its own set of opportunities to participate.
I want to comment on the fundamental objectives in the Throne Speech that present my constituents with both challenges and opportunities. The constituency of Wetaskiwin is very diverse in cultures and economic base, but nevertheless it is very economically active. When I see objectives like building a strong economy, preserving Canada's environment, maintaining a caring, compassionate society, fostering a confident sense of Canada's cultural and national uniqueness, I welcome the opportunity for my constituents to share and participate in the constructive direction of our second mandate.
I want to review each major component of the Throne Speech in retrospect by recalling incidents during the election campaign. With respect to the economy, there were many times when I knocked on doors to find constituents very concerned about the deficit. We have since received calls and letters, as I am sure all my colleagues in the House have, from constituents who say or write: "please do something to reduce the deficit".

With regard to preserving Canada's environment, during the first two or three weeks of my campaign, the number one issue in my constituency was the environment. As we moved to the second half of the campaign, freer trade became the issue.
It is with gratitude that I listened to the Throne Speech, because the most important concerns of my constituency, the economy and the environment, are being addressed by this Government as priorities.
The constituency of Wetaskiwin has some of the most caring and compassionate people in the nation. The family, including children and the elderly, are the strength and base of our communities. Communities like Leduc, Ponoka, Lacombe or Wetaskiwin, communities whether they be urban or rural, agricultural or energy based, all have this same quality of caring and compassion.
In like fashion, Wetaskiwin has the richness of multicultural heritage. My constituency has as diverse a culture as anywhere in the country. The valuable contributions of the German, Swedish, Oriental, Philippine, French and others are evident from one end of the riding to the other. I am proud to say this is possible by working together with the aboriginal people, my people, in Hobbema.
As I listened to the Throne Speech, I was encouraged as I could hear how this Government was planning to involve my constituents in the constructive development of our nation because of its commitment to national unity.
Let me go back for a moment to address some specifics. Shortly after the election, a constituent, Mr. Hitchcock, wrote to me and expressed concerns about the environment. He did so in a manner to remind me of what one of my forebearers said in 1854:
The shining water that moves in the streams and rivers is not just water, but the blood of our ancestors.
If we sell you our land, you must remember that it is sacred and you must teach your children that it is sacred- The rivers are our brothers, they quench our thirst-The air is precious to the red man, for all things share the same breath -the beast, the tree, the man, they all share the same breath -
The Address-Mr. Littlechild
This we know. The earth does not belong to man: man belongs to the earth. This we know. All things are connected like the blood which unites one family. All things are connected.
Whatever befalls the earth, befalls the sons of the earth. Man did not weave the web of life. He is merely a strand in it. Whatever he does to the web, he does to himself-
The white man too shall pass; perhaps sooner than all the other tribes. Continue to contaminate your beds, and you will one night suffocate in your own waste.
These were very prophetic words. I need not mention the Brundtland Commission's reference to native people as being some of the best environmental protectors in the world. That leads me to another aspect of the Throne Speech.
I want to commend the Prime Minister on the inclusion of aboriginal people in the Throne Speech, as we set out on a positive direction for the next few years. I want to refer to the future constitutional development including aboriginal rights. I quote from the Throne Speech:
My Government is concerned that our native peoples participate fully in Canada's economic development prospects and, to this end, will be extending its programs to assist native economic development.
I welcome this, as one who has constituents among the Four Nations of Hobbema, and look forward to both objectives and to taking advantage of opportunities under the Free Trade Agreement. It has long been my personal belief that education and economic development opportunities for my people are the key essentials to meaningful involvement in our nation. It is only with these tools and skills that we can participate and contribute fully as self-reliant Indian Governments.
I want to compliment our Government's initiative to renew its fight against drug abuse. We have seen its devastation in some communities, and I am encouraged by this commitment as I believe preventative programs for young people.
Another initiative I wish to recognize, because of numerous constituents confiding in me during the campaign, is that of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Program. I welcome on behalf of my constituents these changes, especially as more resources will be directed toward active training. To quote again from the Throne Speech:

5. ft 31
The increasing participation of women in the workforce underlines the need for initiatives that promote equality of opportunity in Canada's economic life.
This will now happen. A recent contribution to the Wetaskiwin and District Chamber of Commerce provides a concrete example. They will be training women, who have been out of work, for job re-entry so they can become participants during this second mandate and beyond. There will be greater opportunities for productive and rewarding experience in the workforce. The Wetaskiwin PALS, a Program for Adult Literacy Skills, is encouraged by the literacy initiatives mentioned in the Throne Speech.
There are many more opportunities to which I can make reference. We realize there are also many challenges that face us in the coming years. We have made commitments to a more competitive economy; a human resources development strategy; a commitment to sustainable development; maintaining our social programs; fostering our national identity; a strong action to reduce the deficit; and a constructive approach in our environmental international relations. We welcome these challenges and endorse the plan of objectives as outlined in the Throne Speech because we see a brighter future for Wetaskiwin.

subsubtopic: INCREASED NATURAL GAS EXPORTS
speechtext:
The National Energy Board has to decide on a proposal to export nine trillion cubic feet of natural gas, about 10 per cent of our total supply. The proposal could mean that future generations of Canadians will be deprived of nine million millions cubic feet of gas. We would remain "hewers of wood and drawers of water".
It is unfortunate that this Government seems uninterested in our future needs. It should at least direct the National Energy Board to make approval contingent upon the condition that exported gas would replace and not add to oil or coal burning. Natural gas pollutes less than oil or coal. Therefore, it contributes less to global climate warming.
The proposal before the NEB should not be examined as a request for export in isolation from our long-term interests, but rather in the context of an energy strategy
for Canada with the reduction of global climate warming as a goal.
Unfortunately, this Government is not interested in long-term energy policy, climate warming and the needs of future generations.

Mr. Speaker, on Sunday will begin the National Volunteer Week, during which we should reflect on the tremendous efforts made by the Canadian volunteers to improve our life.
I am very pleased to honour the volunteers in my constituency, especially the people working at the Volunteer Action Center in Orleans and the Help Center 23, as well as all the volunteers helping the chronic and mentally handicapped patients at the Saint-Augustin and Robert-Giffard Hospitals.
In Canada, the economic value of volunteer work is estimated at some $4 billion, which I hope you realize is an outstanding amount! But the true value of these people's work cannot be measured in economic terms. Instead, we are talking here of some irreplaceable efforts made by millions of Canadians who make a point of improving the quality of life in Canada and to build a more human and friendly world.
Mr. Speaker, the National Volunteer Week gives us the opportunity to recognize the wonderful work of Canadian volunteers and the profound influence they have on our society.

Mr. Speaker, the Department of Agriculture, at the request of the food industry, has prepared an information kit designed to link up food processors, producers and distributors with food banks in Canada.
This move indicates that the Government's view of food banks is as a formal and institutionalized component to Canadian social services. It also indicates that the Government is anticipating an increased demand for

food banks because of such policies as the restructuring of the Unemployment Insurance Program.
We are seeing the abrogation of the Government's responsibility to provide jobs and a decent standard of living for Canadians by further relying on the private sector to do a job that rightly belongs to government.
The Government should be putting its resources into programs that will eradicate the need for food banks. Instead, the Government appears to be acknowledging that food banks are an appropriate remedy for its inaction and inability to get Canadians working.
I call on the Government to find ways to end the need for food banks, rather than to look at ways of making them a permanent feature of Canadian life.

Mr. Speaker, there was more killing and bloodshed in the occupied West Bank yesterday.
Surely it is high time for Israel's friends to tell her, in no uncertain terms, that the continual murdering of Palestinian civilians by the Israeli military is cruel, intolerable, and must stop.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) will be aware that Canada has over 100 Native Friendship Centres.
Their primary objective is to improve the quality of life for aboriginal peoples in an urban environment.
The Minister will also be aware that, following the recommendations of a 1988 study, the federal Cabinet, prior to the 1988 federal election, decided to renew the Friendship Centre Program on a permanent basis.
The Government is now in the process of reviewing all program expenditures with a view to budget cuts.
In light of the capping on post-secondary funding for natives, concerns have been raised as to whether or not the funding for these centres might fall prey to the same type of action.
In the event of any reduction in this program, the Minister should know that for every dollar cut by the Government the centres will lose three times that in funds received from other sources to support these centres.
Cuts or reductions in support will affect not only the centres themselves, but the economy of the surrounding communities.
I call upon the Minister to reassure the House that there will be no cuts or reductions of the Friendship Centre Program in the April 27 Budget.

subtopic: CALL FOR END TO STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE
CALL FOR END TO STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to address myself to the native students who are presently on a hunger strike on the issue of the new post-secondary assistance program.
These students should discontinue their hunger strike and meet with the Minister, as he has suggested.
The students are asking for a delay in the implementation of policy, and bilateral negotiations. The Minister has stated that the policy will not be implemented until September, providing time for the discussions that the Minister has begun. He has also emphasized his interest in the presence of student representatives at that table. I feel that the position of the Minister is reasonable and conciliatory.
I know that all Canadians agree that discussions, negotiations, and even demonstrations are legitimate exercises in a democratic society. Hunger strikes and other forms of coercion are not.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to mark the death of Abbie Hoffman, notorious anti-war protester, one of the Chicago Seven, and a leader of that heterogeneous but nevertheless united phenomenon called the counter-culture.
Those of us who were affected, indeed inspired at times by the various philosophical critiques of modern society offered by the counter-culture, and by the creative irreverence and questioning of authority of leaders like Hoffman, may have grown to see that the world is a more complicated reality than we thought, and that even counter-cultures are fraught with pitfalls.

However, I believe there are many in Canada and in the United States who are still living out their opposition to establishment values in their work in the church, in community-based organizations, in development and peace groups, in trade unions, in politics, in education, and in the environmental movement.
We have not forgotten, or closed our eyes to the heart of darkness that lies at the center of a civilization willing to destroy and/or poison the earth, to starve children in order to pay the banks, or to send the young off to be killed in wars to protect the business interests of the corporate elite. We may be more mature now, whatever that means, but we will overcome. Wait for it.

Mr. Speaker, this year, the National Citizenship Week will be held from April 16 to 23.
What better opportunity than to reflect on the tremendous privilege that is ours of living and prospering with complete freedom in our great and beautiful country, a country rich in unique natural, cultural, and human resources.
During the National Citizenship Week, let's not forget to thank and honour the men and women who have built Canada, as well as all the others who keep working hard to make our country a better place to live for our children and grandchildren.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADA INTERVENE WITH GOVERNMENT OF BURUNDI ON BEHALF OF M. REMI GAHUTU
REQUEST THAT CANADA INTERVENE WITH GOVERNMENT OF BURUNDI ON BEHALF OF M. REMI GAHUTU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the House to a clear case of human rights violation and ask the Canadian Government to urge the authorities concerned to stop such violations.
I refer to the case of Mr. Remi Gahutu, President of the Palipehutu, who is the main Leader of the Hutu Opposition in exile and is currently the victim of harassment from the Government in power in Burundi.
We have been advised that the Burundian intelligence services are hunting down refugees abroad, especially in Tanzania, offering bounties and bribes to whoever will persecute them. It is not the first time that Mr. Remi Gahutu is thus subjected to arbitrary arrests and harassment by local Mpanda officials on behalf of the Burundian Government.
I ask therefore the Canadian Government to contact without delay the authorities in Dar-Es-Salaam and insist that they leave Mr. Gahutu and his supporters alone and respect their human rights.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to the attention of colleagues in the House some interesting activities, both past and future, of the international Global Committee of Parliamentarians on Population and Development.
Last April the Global Committee co-sponsored, together with the Temple of Understanding, which is an inter-faith group based in New York, the Oxford Forum of Parliamentarians and spiritual leaders on global survival. This forum was held in Oxford, England, and it was so successful that, in January, 1990, the U.S.S.R. will sponsor a similar meeting in Moscow which will be hosted by an interesting group of three, namely, the Supreme Soviet, the Soviet Academy of Sciences, and the Russian Orthodox Church, to discuss those issues affecting global survival.
There will also be a meeting in Quito, Ecuador, in March, 1990, in which Parliamentarians from the western hemisphere will participate in discussions dealing with the issues of the environment and how that affects population and development.
Of special interest to colleagues in the House, in June, 1989, there will be a seminar on the Hill in Room 200. There will be a dinner and a meeting in the evening where issues of population and development will be discussed.

In a few weeks, Mr. Speaker, the Committee for the economic recovery and employment in South Western Montreal will make public its report on the economic crisis which is now raging in the South Western part of the island.
For a number of years, the industrial base in that area has been deteriorating, with the result that thousands of Montrealers have lost their jobs. This drain must stop.
It is essential first of all to keep the jobs we have, create new ones, foster economic development, implement without delay re-adjustment programs for workers and make sure that the three levels of Government combine their effort to come up with a true industrial policy for that area.
Therefore, I strongly support the CREESOM initiative and the action of such organization as the Association Urgence Sud-Ouest, PEP, as well as the many South-West community groups and unions organizations whose common pupose is to make our elected representatives, the contractors and public generally more aware of challenges to come.

Mr. Speaker, vast investments in fossil fuels ignore the terrible potential consequences of the greenhouse effect. The energy sources of the future must be renewable and non-polluting. To trivialize wind power or solar power, as the Minister of Energy (Mr. Epp) did yesterday in order to justify heavy cuts in alternative energy research is to fail to provide the type of leadership that the country needs.
The discovery of cold hydrogen fusion, if confirmed, places every nation with electrical power and water and a commitment to research and development on the same
starting line. With the potential development of a revolutionary technology it is no overstatement to say that it could prolong the very existence of the earth.
It is a real commitment to research and development that Canada lacks. I have asked the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Winegard) to begin consultations so that Canada can be ready when the race begins for the development of practical fusion technology. I now ask when will the Minister answer, and what will he answer? Will he resort to the trivializing ignorance of his colleague in energy or will he show the foresight that science requires but which is so politically rare?
Shall Canadian creativity at last be unleashed? Or will we be in the grandstand watching the race for a place in creating a sustainable economic future for mankind? Our scientists, our industry, our workers, and our nation await an answer.

Mr. Speaker, in my riding of Parkdale-High Park, and in every other city in Canada that has an apartment building with a superintendent couple, women are being treated as second-class citizens.
Mrs. Alma Weaver signed a contract with Cadillac-Fairview guaranteeing that she would do the work as specified in the contract and that she would not take a job outside the home. Although she works side by side with her husband, she was not paid a salary. Therefore she was unable to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan, unemployment insurance, or the company pension.
The largest and fastest growing group of people who live under the poverty line is made up of single, widowed and divorced women over the age of 65. If Mrs. Weaver were to lose her husband in any circumstance she would be forced to join this group, because the owners of the building were allowed to hire two people and pay benefits and salary to only one.
What protection has the Minister of Employment provided in her UI changes for the protection of thousands of women like Alma Weaver who is the urban version of the farm wife?

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Thrner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: BENEFITS INCREASE ANNOUNCED PRIOR TO ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Prime Minister but in his absence perhaps the Deputy Prime Minister would address himself to it.
This week we finally saw the ugly side of members of the Conservative Cabinet. They have broken their election promises, what the Minister of Finance called commitments. They have misled the country. They have been complete hypocrites on serious constitutional issues. They are playing tough guys with a group of students who are lying ill on a hunger strike. They have launched a savage attack on the unemployed of the country.
Their harsh agenda is no longer hidden. Canadians are finally seeing the real Tory Party.
Since the Prime Minister refuses to tell us whether he authorized the Minister for International Trade to tell the people of Newfoundland and the people of Canada that there would be no changes to the unemployment insurance scheme, will the Deputy Prime Minister tell us whether the Prime Minister authorized the Minister of Employment to raise benefits for the unemployed just six days before the last general election?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: BENEFITS INCREASE ANNOUNCED PRIOR TO ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has been spreading all sorts of information around this week which bears no resemblance to reality.
First, the announcement during the election was the normal annual announcement made by the Unemployment Insurance Commission which relates premiums to average industrial earnings. That was the announcement that was made last November, as it is made every November, and as it will be made next November.
The program that we have announced involves a reallocation of $1.29 billion for the benefit of the unemployed. It is an approach that was advocated by a committee of this House which presented a unanimous report whose authors included Members from the opposite side of the House who suggested to the Govern
ment that we should extend the training benefits and the active uses of unemployment insurance.
When will the Hon. Member stick to the facts and the history?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last November's announcement was authorized and even made by the Minister. The Government has just shown all the electoral cynicism it displayed on the subject of unemployment insurance benefits. I would like to know whether the Government will also show the same cynicism regarding premiums-yesterday, it was benefits; today, it is premiums-paid into the unemployment insurance fund by workers in our country? On November 15, the same day, the Conservative Government reduced by 17 per cent the unemployment insurance premiums that employers and employees have to pay in Canada. In effect, that corresponds to a tax reduction which can amount to $184 on the premiums paid for all Canadian workers.
Can the Minister give us the assurance that no change will be made to these premiums, which were reduced in November, in the Finance Minister's Budget?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is the Leader of the Liberal Party who is cynical because in the debate in 1984, he said: "We must maintain our unemployment insurance systems. They must be converted to some extent into training and retraining. We must update our concepts."

As I said last time, the Minister has to read the whole quotation. I said that it must never be done on the backs of the unemployed and that training must be the responsibility of employers or the Canadian Government, depending on its income. That was the question.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF PREMIUMS-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PAYMENT OF PREMIUMS-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address my question to the Deputy Prime Minister since obviously the Minister does not choose to respond to questions. She comes up with a line.

I know that the Minister of Finance will not customarily reveal his budget posture. However, the Prime Minister allowed the Minister of Employment to cut premiums paid by working Canadians on unemployment insurance, premiums paid by the employers and the employees, during the election campaign, by 17 per cent. The Minister does not appear ready to honour that commitment in this House. The Minister of Finance will not reveal, obviously, what he wants to say in the Budget. But the Tory Government cut those premiums paid by workers by 17 per cent six days before the election.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister guarantee us and Canadians that at least this election commitment will be kept by the Minister of Finance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: PAYMENT OF PREMIUMS-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE
speechtext: The Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker, knows full well what the formula is for the premium structure in unemployment insurance and that an independent commission has a mandate to establish the premiums. They have been doing that every year, Mr. Speaker, going back into the mists of time. The Leader of the Opposition knows full well that any changes to funding, any kind of funding, come in a budget, but the legitimate changes that were made last fall were made by an independent unemployment insurance commission, just as they have been done through years and years of unemployment insurance.

subsubtopic: POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION-STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs on the unfair practices of the Government with respect to native post-secondary education. Last night I met with several chiefs from the riding of Kenora- Rainy River. People have come from across Canada to support native students who are in their twenty-fourth day of fasting. Can the Minister tell me how I can explain to those Chiefs who have travelled great distances to Ottawa what he means by his words:
There is no need for them to continue in this dangerous and essentially undemocratic undertaking.
Oral Questions
How can the Minister say this when nothing has been resolved? Why, Mr. Speaker, do people in this country have to go to extremes to get their message across to this Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION-STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate to all Members of this House, to all Canadians and particularly to the native students that are involved in the hunger strike, that they do not have to resort to a hunger strike to have meetings with me. My hon. friend may have met with some Chiefs last night, Mr. Speaker. I have met with Chiefs also. I have met twice with Grand Chief Erasmus and a representation of 12 or 13 other Chiefs from across Canada. We have discussed this issue. Unfortunately there is no resolution to date because their demand is unreasonable.

subsubtopic: POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION-STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION-STUDENTS' HUNGER STRIKE
speechtext: All I am asking is that they do put an end to the hunger strike, that they sit down with me and discuss this policy which I am prepared to discuss with them, this policy that they themselves find unreasonable. First Nations find Circular E-12, which is the old policy, to be unacceptable and totally inconsistent with the principle of First Nations' jurisdiction over education. We agree, Mr. Speaker. We have got new guidelines that are more generous, and I am prepared to look into them again. If they can improve, we will certainly look into it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary to the same Minister. We have sat here in the last few weeks and listened to this rhetoric over and over again. I would like to ask the Minister today to give us a hand and commit himself to begin a bilateral process with the Indian people, without restrictions on time and demonstrate respect on behalf of all the people in this House to the native peoples and First Nations of our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, who is getting entangled in which rhetoric. If the Hon. Member, and the others who are yelling across the floor, have been listening to what I have said, I have already indicated that I am prepared to sit down and discuss the new guidelines. In my mind bilateral means that there will be representatives of my Department and/or myself and representatives of the native students and/or the Chiefs obviously. That is bilateral. That is

what I have been saying, and that is to what I am committed. As soon as the students put an end to their hunger strike, come and meet with me. My door is open.

My
question is also to the Minister of Indian Affairs. As we have heard, Mr. Speaker, this is the twenty-fourth day of a fast by 16 young Canadians. I trust that I speak for all Canadians when I say that this is a situation that cries out for resolution. Would the Minister confirm that, upon receiving notification that the fast has ended, he will initiate a substantive and effective bilateral process of consultation and ensure that this process includes recognized representatives of both the Indian leadership of this country and of the students, confirm that there is no predetermined cap on future funding and that it is his intention to seek such funding within the budgetary framework as required to meet the demand? Will he include an effective mechanism to address the treaty applications of this issue within the bilateral process and ensure that during the interim period no individual Indian students will be worse off than they would have been under the old guidelines?

I agree with First Nations when they say that the E-12 document, the old policy, obstructs rather than facilitates post-secondary education for First Nation students. thank the Minister for his response, but I was wondering did the points which I in fact outlined represent his position? If they do, do they also represent the position of the Government?

subsubtopic: FUNDS REDIRECTED TO TRAINING-EXPENDITURE LOCATIONS
speechtext:
My
question, Mr. Speaker, is for the Minister for Employment. Under the existing Unemployment Insurance Program, the legislation assures that the Unemployment Insurance Fund, that is unemployment insurance money, will go to unemployed workers in the regions where they live, very often the regions with the highest unemployment. Under her new proposals, what will she do as Minister to assure that the $800 million redirected to training and human resource planning will go to these same individuals, the unemployed in Canada, in the provinces where they live? Will she put this requirement in the law as it now is, or will this targeting be left to the discretion of the Minister, which means the money could end up very often in the high growth areas of the country rather than go to the underdeveloped areas of the country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: FUNDS REDIRECTED TO TRAINING-EXPENDITURE LOCATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me point out, for example, that the money going into Newfoundland as a region will be higher under this program than it is under the old program.
The training under unemployment insurance is voluntary. We are not forcing people to take training. We are saying that we will provide accessibility to training under this program, which people will want to take. We will do it under the Community Futures Program which benefits the high unemployment regions in this country, as we have been doing under the Canadian Jobs Strategy. The funds will be directed to those who have the greatest need.

subsubtopic: FUNDS REDIRECTED TO TRAINING-EXPENDITURE LOCATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, she is taking $800 million out of the fund and redirecting it to matters that are not purely protection for the unemployed. There is no assurance that that $800 million will go back to the provinces and the people who need it most.

Will she agree to refer the White Paper she has produced this week to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration as quickly as possible early next week, with a mandate to have a wide range of hearings across the country on this important matter that touches all Canadians?

subsubtopic: REPORT ON MEAT HYGIENE
speechtext: My question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. I want to ask the Minister what action he is taking as a result of the previously secret document on meat hygiene revealed yesterday. This report is a startling document. It suggests that 2.5 million Canadians become ill each year, several hundred die, and losses to the Canadian economy in terms of wages, health care costs and human suffering are over $1 billion. I want to ask the Minister what action he is planning to take as a result of this document?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REPORT ON MEAT HYGIENE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, this food advisory safety committee was structured in 1986. It was made up of the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Health, consumer groups, unions and members of the industrial sector to look at safety standards, risks associated with the handling of food, and the inspection program.
Oral Questions
If the Member wants to refer to the report, perhaps he might want to look at its conclusions. The report concludes that the observation of the committee was that the meat hygiene program is detecting the problems and adequately giving assurance that wholesome meat supply is reaching the Canadian public. It went on to say that there remains a great deal to be done in the area of food-borne disease incidents in Canada, which is not within the mandate of the hygiene program, especially as it relates to the handling of the product at home and in the food preparation area. It said the spread of many food-borne diseases may be prevented by proper cooking and handling of foods.
The conclusion of the advisory committee regarding the hygiene inspection division is that wholesome meat is reaching the Canadian public.

Of the 14 diseases covered in this report, which was secret until yesterday, I want to ask the Minister about the problem of salmonella infection. The report suggests that half of those people suffering from salmonellosis, some 313,000, are due to the meat inspection regime in this country. The losses involve almost $400 million, and some 300 deaths occur. The report makes recommendations about what should be done about salmonella infection in this country with regard to meat inspection.
With regard to this one disease, can the Minister say he has implemented the recommendations of the report?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I want to repeat again the findings of the advisory committee. The committee said, and I quote: "Agriculture Canada is ensuring that wholesome meat is reaching the Canadian public". For the Hon. Member to stand up and sensationalize and dramatize this issue not based on facts, based on misinterpretation and erroneous conclusions, is an unfortunate situation. It does not do a great service to the agricultural industry.
With respect to salmonella, three years ago Agriculture Canada and Health and Welfare created a co-ordinating committee to look at critical points such as processing plants, hatcheries and feed mills where contamination could occur. The committee looked at ways and means of reducing the opportunity for this to happen. An action plan was implemented. As the Auditor General said in his report, 95 per cent of the action plan has been completed. There have been increased inspections. The Auditor General pointed out he was impressed by the dedication of the Food Production and

Oral Questions
Inspection Branch management and the inspection staff and the high regard in which the branch is held internationally. That should give the Hon. Member confidence. I am sure it gives Canadians confidence as well.

USE OF DRUGS BY ATHLETES-UNITED STATES-SOVIET UNION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport. The United States and the Soviet Union recently entered into an agreement allowing for the testing of each other's athletes for illegal performance-enhancing drugs. speechtext:
I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Stormont-Dundas on his election and his appointment as associate critic for fitness and amateur sport.
The issue of doping is extremely important in Canada. It was important for this Government in 1985 when we brought in the first policy, one of the most severe domestic policies in the world, in the area of anti-doping. In 1987 the Government brought forward an anti-doping strategy under the leadership of the then Minister of Health and Welfare that affords a multi-dimensional approach. In June of 1988 we had the first international anti-doping conference in this country due to the leadership of my predecessor. We have played a leadership role in the world. We intend to pursue that leadership role. We will look closely at any association we can enter into that will help Canada and this Government fight doping in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am neither the critic nor associate critic. I am a co-critic.
In a recent poll, 87 per cent indicated support for frequent and surprise random drug testing and for Canadian amateur athletes, especially before an international competition. Given the results of this survey, I want to ask the Minister if he will act immediately and announce Canada's willingness to join this program?

little intrigued. When the Member for Stormont-Dundas and his colleague are together, does that make them co-co's?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The bank rate rose by some ten bases points yesterday. Real interest rates are at the same level as they were in 1981 when this country went into a recession from which many Canadians have not yet recovered. I want the Minister of Finance to explain why he is stubbornly insisting on repeating the Liberal mistakes of 1981 and 1982? Why has he not urged the Bank of Canada to bring down interest rates in this country in order to avert and avoid another recession? Why is he acting like Allan MacEa-chen?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are doing precisely the opposite of what the Hon. Member is saying we are doing. We are not repeating the same mistakes. The previous mistakes were made in the 1970s when inflation was allowed to get out of control. That led to the problems we ran into in the early 1980s.

The Hon. Member is asking me to ask the Governor of the Bank of Canada to print more money when today we are reminded that inflation is running at high levels. We must ensure we stop inflation from getting out of hand. If we allow it to get out of hand by printing more money, then yes, we will have the same problem we had in 1981 and 1982.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK RATE
speechtext: In 1981, the Minister of Finance, who was then in opposition, said a high interest rate policy would provoke a recession in this country. Now he is nothing more than the clone of Allan MacEachen.

Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago, the provincial premiers, including that friend of the Government of Canada, Robert Bourassa, called for lower interest rates in Canada. And yesterday, the Canadian Catholic bishops asked for exactly the same thing. My question is: Can the Minister now explain to the House why he does not listen to the provincial premiers, why he does not listen to the bishops of Canada, and could he now explain how high he intends to let interest rates rise before acting for the Canadian people?

Mr. Speaker, I do listen to the Premiers. I do listen to the Catholic Bishops. I will listen to the advice of anybody who cares to provide me with advice. However, at the end of the road we must decide how to take that advice and how to use that advice. All the advice that is coming to us from those particular quarters can only be interpreted as saying "print more money".
Printing more money will not solve the inflation problem. It will compound the inflation problem. Compounding the inflation problem will lead to higher interest rates. Higher interest rates will lead to the problems that we ran into in 1981 and 1982, and then the high levels of unemployment and the serious recession that we had at that time. That is precisely what we are trying to avoid.
